items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: That's where Muddy Waters, and all those kind of people -- Blind John, all those people; Willie Dixon, they had that territory.

ctx.x: Joe's been on top of the music scene in Chicago for years, you know; like -- see, Chicago was kind of split up. There was the north side, west side, and the south side. You don't really have no east side; it's east now, but all the real, I would say, swinging stuff was out the south side and maybe further north. Got around Argyle then, you know -- Lawrence Avenue, white clubs and what not.

Then on the west side of Chicago, you had all the and Howling Wolf blues joints. That's where Muddy Waters, and all those kind of people -- Blind John, all those people; Willie Dixon, they had that territory. And you would go and play a gig on the west side, and people wouldn't accept you -- there were a few diehard jazz lovers, but if you weren't playing the harmonica, Spitoon Blues, you was in trouble.

I got to tell you this, though ... this happened, I think before Sonny Rollins -- this happened in '55, after I left Griffin. The little guitar player I was raised up with out in Chicago, Leo Blevins, a little short dude -- he would come and stay right on top of everybody that played.
